title: 'Boundary Has to Be Stable': Jaishankar Sets Condition for Normal China Ties
excerpt: At the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in Delhi, India's foreign minister tied normalisation with China to a quiet border, while keeping investment and market access as separate tracks.
body:
• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said peace and tranquillity in the border areas are essential to normalising India-China relations, and any disturbance would have consequences.
  • He noted that no blood was shed on the border from 1975 to 2020, that the 2020 clash broke that pattern, and that restoring calm took four years of negotiations.
  • As border areas have settled since 2024, Jaishankar said, the wider relationship is moving commensurately toward normalcy.
  • He separated the boundary question from business: Chinese investment and market-access issues will be dealt with separately, while India presses its complaint that its firms do not get a level playing field in China.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar has set out India's condition for normal relations with China in plain terms: the boundary must stay stable. Speaking in Delhi in a conversation with John Micklethwait, editor-in-chief of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Jaishankar said peace and tranquillity in the border areas were essential to normalising ties, and that any disturbance along the border would have consequences, according to NDTV's syndicated report.

"The boundary has to be stable."

— S. Jaishankar, External Affairs Minister

45 Quiet Years, Then 2020

Jaishankar framed the dispute as a long-standing one. India and China have no agreed border, he said, and the issue has persisted for decades. From 1975 until 2020 — a span of 45 years — no blood was shed on that border, and during that period the broader relationship grew.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=CIguj0QGYgY

That changed in 2020, during the COVID lockdown, when a series of border issues culminated in a clash in which soldiers were killed on both sides. Jaishankar called it a profound departure from the situation that had prevailed since 1975. The consequences, he said, were visible for the following five years, and restoring peace and tranquillity took four years of negotiations.

Normalcy Follows the Border

India's message to Beijing, as Jaishankar described it, is that if China wants a normal relationship and wants the rest of the relationship to move, the boundary has to be stable — a point he characterised as common sense. As the border areas have settled down to a great extent since 2024, he said, the relationship is moving commensurately toward normalcy.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2110090718467575975

He made a similar assessment in September at an Asia Society conversation in New York, where he said ties were better than in preceding years and improving as outstanding border issues are progressively resolved. The Delhi remarks extend that line: normalisation is real, but it remains conditional on the border staying quiet.

Business Kept Separate — With Conditions

Asked whether India would consider allowing greater Chinese investment if an early-harvest agreement were reached, Jaishankar said the possibilities are an active conversation, but clarified that investment and market-access policies would be addressed separately from the boundary issue. India is not insisting, he said, that the boundary be solved before business can be done; the lower bar is maintaining peace and tranquillity.

That openness comes with a grievance. Jaishankar pointed to major economic problems in the relationship: a trade balance he described as completely and extremely one-sidedly tilted, and sectors in which Indian firms have succeeded elsewhere but have not obtained market access or run successful operations in China. India, he said, does not believe it is getting a level playing field in China of the kind it has given Chinese firms.

What to Watch

The practical tests now sit in two places. On the border, whether the calm that has held since 2024 continues through future negotiating rounds. On the economic side, whether the active conversation on investment produces specific openings — and whether India links any of them to progress on market access for its own companies. Jaishankar's formulation gives both sides room to move on business while keeping the strategic condition unchanged.
